newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's CRH upbeat despite profit warning.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's CRH upbeat despite profit warning.

text.p: Irish building materials group CRH Plc said on Wednesday it expected further growth this year after a good start across its businesses but warned that first-half profits would be marginally weaker.

"We look forward to a further year of growth...However, group profits for the half year, reflecting higher financing costs of 1996 acquisitions and the seasonal North American trading pattern, will be slightly lower," chairman Tony Barry told shareholders at the annual meeting.

Chief executive Don Godson said the company, one of Ireland's largest with 19,000 employees world-wide and pretax profits last year of 193 million Irish pounds ($290 million), was still on course for higher full-year profits.

He said the expected lower first-half profit was "not a problem" and would not derail CRH's plans for more strategic acquisitions in Europe and the U.S. Some 20 million Irish pounds of acquisitions had already been completed this year and more were in the pipeline, he said.
CRH shares were little moved by the warning, slipping three Irish pence to 680 in Dublin.

Dealers said CRH had already signalled that profitability at its newly-enlarged north American group, which accounts for 42 percent of 2.4 billion Irish pounds of group sales, was skewed towards the second half of the year.
"This reflects the tough winters prevailing in their main markets from which these businesses profit through repair and remediation," Barry said.
CRH made its largest-ever acquisition last year, buying U.S. construction materials group Tilcon for $329 million to strengthen its foothold in the north-eastern United States.
Barry said conditions there were still generally favourable and the integration of U.S. units Tilcon, Jack B. Parson and Allied Building Products was proceeding to plan.
He said CRH had made good progress on the sale of surplus Tilcon assets with over $30 million of the planned $50 million of disposals already achieved.
Elsewhere, Barry said construction business growth in Ireland in the year to date had exceeded expectations, with strong demand from the residential, commercial and industrial sectors.
Barry said there were signs of improving demand in recent weeks in Britain, which, including Northern Ireland, accounts for almost one fifth of group turnover.
CRH's operations in the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg had got off to a strong start with more normal winter conditions than the exceptionally hard winter of 1996, he said.

But in continental Europe, which takes around a quarter of sales, markets in Germany and France remained difficult while price pressure persisted in Spain despite stronger demand, Barry told shareholders.
